sources.title: Fioralba Cakoni, David Colton, and Houssem Haddar, Inverse Scattering Theory and Transmission Eigenvalues, CBMS-NSF Regional Conference Series in Applied Mathematics 88
sources.locator: Chapter 1, §1.2, printed pp. 9–11 (Theorems 1.9–1.11, the Lippmann–Schwinger equation, far-field formula and Born approximation); §1.2.2, printed pp. 18–20 (Theorems 1.20–1.22 and the derivative discussion).

contents.name: Theorem 1.9: equivalence between the scattering PDE and the Lippmann–Schwinger equation
contents.reason: The authored Definition stipulates the integral-equation model and does not claim its equivalence to the classical scattering PDE.

contents.name: Theorem 1.10: small-wavenumber uniqueness under a support-radius and contrast-size condition
contents.reason: Its sufficient condition is not the operator-norm hypothesis used here, so it cannot replace or enlarge the locally proved small-norm branch.

contents.name: Theorem 1.11: all-wavenumber uniqueness for the classical refractive-index scattering model
contents.reason: The theorem has a different physical regularity setting; this batch makes no global uniqueness claim and does not import it for L-infinity contrasts.

contents.name: Equation (1.22) and the following weak-scattering Born approximation
contents.reason: The first Born far-field integral is included in the local Born item; the item adds an explicit operator-norm remainder and proves the derivative independently.

contents.name: Theorem 1.20: recovery of the refractive index from full fixed-frequency far-field data
contents.reason: This is a global inverse-uniqueness theorem for complete angular data, while the authored claim is only a local forward-map linearization.

contents.name: Theorem 1.21: Fréchet differentiability of the classical scattering map
contents.reason: The theorem treats general contrast differentiability and cites an external proof; the local derivative at zero is proved independently under different L-infinity hypotheses.

contents.name: Theorem 1.22: injectivity of the derivative in the classical scattering model
contents.reason: Derivative injectivity is not part of the assigned conclusion, and the source itself refers to an external proof for this theorem.

sources.title: Otmar Scherzer and Leonidas Mindrinos, Inverse Problems: Lecture Notes, University of Vienna, Sommersemester 2015
sources.locator: Chapter 5, §5.2.6, printed pp. 79–82; Theorem 5.27, the complete Theorem 5.28 proof, Theorem 5.29 and the complete Theorem 5.30 proof.

contents.name: Theorem 5.27: regularity of the volume potential for smooth compactly supported input
contents.reason: Its smooth-input regularity conclusion is not needed for the L2 volume operator or the local far-field bound used in this batch.

contents.name: Theorem 5.28: equivalence of the smooth scattering problem and its volume integral equation
contents.reason: The authored Definition states the volume-equation convention only and does not assert equivalence with the smooth C2 scattering PDE.

contents.name: Theorem 5.29: unique continuation for a classical refractive-index equation
contents.reason: Unique continuation is not used in the small-norm Neumann argument or in any authored inverse-scattering conclusion.

contents.name: Theorem 5.30: all-wavenumber existence, uniqueness and continuous dependence
contents.reason: This global theorem belongs to the smooth classical scattering model; no global uniqueness or stability claim is transferred to L-infinity contrasts.

sources.title: Semyon Dyatlov, MIT 18.155 Lecture Notes: Distributions, Elliptic Regularity, and Applications to PDEs
sources.locator: Chapter 11, §11.1.1, Definition 11.1 and Proposition 11.2, printed p. 119.

contents.name: Definition 11.1: L1 Fourier transform with kernel exp(-i x·ξ)
contents.reason: After the stated 2pi frequency rescaling, this L1 Fourier-transform definition is included in the fixed-frequency data Definition.

contents.name: Proposition 11.2: continuity of the L1 Fourier transform
contents.reason: Fourier continuity is not needed for the item claims; continuity of the physical far-field in observation direction is supplied by the volume far-field lemma.
